verdict: This is a well-voiced, regionally sound syllabus wearing a Hindi syllabus's clothes, and the borrowed skeleton costs it more than the good judgement earns. The LatAm calls are consistently right and often better than a textbook's: ustedes with no vosotros, manejar/carro/celular, tomar over beber, prender over encender, mostrar over enseñar, la carta against el menú, boleto and pasaje, en la noche, cuarto para las tres, la plata, the coger warning, the correct demotion of the present perfect, and a ser/estar and gustar-frame treatment that is genuinely strong. Three things undermine it. First, holes no Spanish-first curriculum would leave: estar has no headword of its own, and neither do hay, comer, necesitar, pagar, seguir, quedarse or terminar; there is not one pronunciation item in 1,154 slots (five vowels, r against rr, ll/j/h/ñ, seseo, the stress-and-accent rule) even though pronunciation is what decides whether a British adult is understood; there is no article item and no reflexive paradigm despite half a dozen reflexive verbs being taught; and the traveller's whole failure surface is missing (propina, mesero, para llevar, cerveza, restaurante, habitación, cuadra, parada, ¿Cómo llego a…?, Me robaron, embajada, seguro, papel higiénico, damas/caballeros). Second, waste: roughly seventy slots are straight duplicates (el café, el taxi, la cocina, cocinar, querer, nosotros, cero, rápido, el celular, Buenos días, joven three times, don and doña across five entries, and the entire salsa/chile/plátano/limón/empanada/mantequilla block repeated), plus five N/A placeholders that exist only to answer a question about Hindi. Third, residue: about thirty learner-facing notes explain Spanish by contrast with Hindi (कल, ने, पता, दीदी, भाभी, roti, dal, mithai, the auto-rickshaw, cricket, and a note that literally says 'this slot goes to'), which is dead text for this learner and reads as an unfinished port. Tiering is broadly defensible but food-heavy at the top, with sal, leche, verduras and papa at tier 1 while por sits at 2 and pagar does not exist, and it carries one flat contradiction in beber at tier 1 under a note saying nobody uses it. Finally a data bug worth fixing before audio or cards are generated: the roman column is vestigial for a Latin-script language and is accent-stripped for the first 770 entries, so it prints sí as si, más as mas and tú as tu, teaching the exact confusions the notes warn against; mirror the word field or drop the column. Fix the four structural things and this is a very good syllabus; as it stands it is a good one built on the wrong frame.

items.note: Spanish splits 'is' in two: es (ser, identity) vs está (estar, state or location). Es mi amigo. Está aquí.
one word does both jobs, and it sits before the verb: no sé.
accent matters: sí (yes) vs si (if).
usually left out, since the verb ending already says who: hablo = I speak.
the default with strangers, staff and elders across LatAm. Takes third-person verbs: usted habla.
accented when asking: ¿Qué es? Unaccented que = that.
usted takes es, ustedes takes son. Son las tres = it is three o'clock.
soy for who you are; estoy for how or where you are.
esto is the neuter, used for anything not yet identified: ¿Qué es esto?
Spanish keeps 'he/she' and 'that' apart: él and ella for people, ese/esa (near you) or aquel (over there) for things. Plural ellos/ellas.
does possession and origin: la casa de Ana, soy de Londres. de + el contracts to del.
covers all three: en la mesa, en casa, en México.

items.en: to; (personal a) before a person as object
items.note: voy a México; and obligatory before a human object: veo a María. a + el contracts to al.
the other half of the por/para pair: por = cause, means or route; para = purpose or destination. por favor, por aquí, por eso.
everyday 'on the table' is en la mesa; sobre adds 'on top of' or 'concerning'.
becomes e before a word starting i- or hi-: madre e hija.
the all-purpose spoken filler and softener: pues sí, pues no sé. entonces = so/then in a sequence.
nosotras if the group is all women; usually dropped, since -amos says it.
Argentina, Uruguay and much of Central America say vos instead. The plural is always ustedes, never vosotros.
eres for who you are, estás for how you are: eres inglés, estás cansado.
the h is silent. Works at any hour; buenos días / buenas tardes are the fuller versions.
vale is Spain only. LatAm says está bien, bueno, or dale in the Southern Cone.
also the all-purpose 'well...' opener, and how Mexicans answer the phone.
in a negative sentence it flips to tampoco: yo tampoco = me neither.
one verb for both. Irregular yo form: hago. Also weather: hace calor.
the single biggest hurdle in Spanish: ser for who or what something is, estar for how or where it is.
voy, vas, va, vamos, van. ir a + infinitive is the everyday future: voy a comer.
vengo, vienes, viene. ¡Ven! = come here.
-er and -ir verbs run como / comes / come / comemos / comen. No vosotros form in LatAm, so five slots, not six.
agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: mi hijo, mis hijos.
one word doing four jobs. Speech adds de usted / de él when it would be unclear.
sits before the verb: me gusta, me duele, me lo da.

items.en: to you (usted); to him; to her
items.note: te is the tú version. ¿Le ayudo? = shall I help you?
¿Quién es? Plural ¿Quiénes son?
adónde for movement: ¿Adónde vas? ¿Dónde queda...? is very LatAm for places.
accent only in questions.
two words with an accent for the question; porque, one word no accent, is 'because'.
¿Cómo? on its own = sorry, what? Mexico says ¿Mande?
agrees: ¿Cuántos años tienes? ¿Cuánta agua?
acá is just as common in LatAm and slightly vaguer: ven acá.
ahí = right there, near you; allá / allí = further off.
ahorita in Mexico and Central America can mean 'right now' or 'in a while' – tone decides.
the workhorse: ya voy = I'm on my way, ya está = that's it, ya no = not any more. ahora mismo = this very minute.
hoy en día = these days.
mañana is both 'tomorrow' and 'morning': mañana por la mañana. ayer, and anoche for last night.
hasta luego = see you later. después = afterwards.
muy before adjectives and adverbs (muy bueno, muy bien); mucho with nouns and after verbs (mucho trabajo, me gusta mucho).
un poquito is softer and far commoner in speech. un poco de agua.
demasiado = too much. más o menos = more or less, and the standard reply to 'how are you?'
poco = little, few. al menos = at least.
the shop and restaurant reply: ¿Algo más? – Nada más, gracias. Also means 'just': nada más quiero ver.
todo el día, todos los días. todo el mundo = everybody.
¿Algo más? algunos = some, out of a group.
nadie = nobody; algún / alguna = any, some.
singular in Spanish: la gente dice, la gente es amable.

items.en: the matter; the topic; the thing
items.note: masculine despite the -a. Ese es el tema = that's the thing. el asunto is the formal twin.
trabajar = to work. la chamba (Mexico) and el laburo (Argentina) are the slangy versions.
en casa = at home, with no article. a casa = homewards.
el apellido = surname. In speech you ask with llamarse, not nombre.
feminine but takes el to avoid two a-sounds: el agua fría, las aguas.
The drink you will be offered in every home and office. el té = tea, and ¿un cafecito? is the friendly version.
comer = to eat. In Mexico la comida is also the main midday meal.
la plata is the everyday spoken word for cash across much of LatAm. el efectivo = cash as opposed to card.
also means weather. Clock time is la hora: ¿Qué hora es? An occasion is la vez: otra vez.
las cosas = stuff, one's things. ¿Cómo van las cosas?
el sitio is just as common. en lugar de = instead of.
doy, das, da. ¿Me da...? is the standard way to ask for something in a shop.

items.en: to take; to drink; to catch (a bus)
items.note: the LatAm workhorse: tomar un taxi, tomar un café. llevar = take something somewhere; agarrar = grab.
veo, ves, ve. a ver = let's see. nos vemos = see you.
oír is 'hear' strictly, escuchar is 'listen', but LatAm speech uses escuchar for both: no te escucho.
fully regular, and the model for every -ar verb.
digo, dices, dice, decimos, dicen. ¿Cómo se dice...? = how do you say...?

items.en: to meet (first time); to know (a person or place)
items.note: conozco, conoces. Mucho gusto en conocerte. Pairs against saber, which is for facts.

items.en: to know (a fact); to know how to
items.note: sé, sabes, sabe. saber for facts and skills, conocer for people and places. ¿Sabes nadar?
¿Cuál es la dirección? It also means 'direction'. For a street number, el número; for the postcode, el código postal.
entiendo, entiendes, entiende. ¿Me entiende? comprender is the formal twin.
¿Dónde vives? quedarse = to stay: me quedo en el hotel.
quiero, quieres, quiere. Softer in a shop: quisiera. necesitar = to need. te quiero = I love you.
in LatAm speech tomar is far commoner: ¿Qué va a tomar?
andar covers 'go about' and 'work, function': el carro no anda; ¿cómo andas?
Spanish hacer already covers both 'do' and 'make'; preparar is for food, drinks and plans.
pongo, pones, pone. ponerse = put clothes on; guardar = to keep, store away.
-ar verbs flip to -e for usted, -er and -ir verbs flip to -a: come / coma / coman. Irregular tú forms: ven, ten, pon, di, haz.
vámonos = let's get out of here. ¡Dale! or ¡Órale! (Mexico) do the 'come on then' job.
¡Pase, pase! at a door. Mexico says pásele. tú: pasa.
tú: siéntate. Tome asiento is the formal version.
handing something over. tú: ten, or toma. Also tome.
inviting someone to speak, at a counter or on the phone. tú: dime. Also ¿Qué se le ofrece?
does both jobs: flagging a stranger down and apologising lightly. tú: disculpa.
the instant sorry when you bump into someone. lo siento is heavier, for real regret or bad news.
goes at the end far more often than at the start. porfa is the clipped friendly version.
answering an apology. Answering thanks: de nada, or no hay de qué.
The polite acceptance of an offer. To an older stranger, sí, señora or sí, señor is warmer still, and cómo no is the enthusiastic yes.
the polite refusal, and the one you will need most as a guest.
estar, not ser. tú: ¿cómo estás? Casual: ¿qué tal? ¿cómo te va?
estoy for a state. Bien, gracias, ¿y usted? is the full move.
tú: ¿y tú?
¿Qué pasa? = what's going on. In Mexico ¿Qué pasó? doubles as a friendly hello.
esto is the neuter form, used precisely because you do not yet know what it is.
literally 'I call myself'. Mi nombre es ... is stiffer and rarer in speech.
tú: ¿cómo te llamas?
Spanish 'has' hunger: tener hambre, sed, frío, calor, sueño, prisa.
tener que + infinitive = have to. Softer: ya me voy.
sino replaces it after a negative: no es caro sino barato.
becomes u before a word starting o- or ho-: siete u ocho.
one word, no accent. Contrast ¿por qué? = why.
surprise, pain or dismay: ¡Ay, no! ¡Ay, qué pena!
shortens before a noun: un café, una cerveza.
mi mamá is what people actually say; madre is formal or emphatic. Stress the second syllable.
stress the second syllable: papá. el papa (first syllable) is the Pope, la papa is the potato.
los hermanos = siblings generally.
mijo and mija, worn down from mi hijo, are the affectionate 'love, dear' to someone younger.

items.en: miss (young woman; a waitress or shop assistant)
items.note: How you address a younger woman you do not know, in a shop or a café. For an older woman, señora.

items.en: young man (hailing a waiter or shop assistant)
items.note: Mexico and Central America hail a young man or a waiter with ¡joven! whatever his age; elsewhere ¡amigo! or ¡señor!
a real caring question from hosts and family in LatAm, but not a greeting the way Hindi's is. usted: ¿ya comió?
un poquito de español is friendlier still.
fuller: ¿Puede hablar más despacio?
quick versions: ¿Cómo? or ¿Mande? in Mexico. Otra vez, por favor.
also ¡Ah, ya! on its own.
about something just said: no entendí.

items.en: how do you say this in Spanish?
items.note: the single most useful sentence you can carry. ¿Qué significa? = what does it mean?
called el castellano in Argentina, Chile, Peru and Bolivia.

items.en: for; in order to; to (a destination)
items.note: purpose and destination; por is cause and means. para mí, para llevar = takeaway.
fuses with pronouns: conmigo, contigo. sin = without.
Spanish owns things with a plain verb: tengo dos hijos, tengo tiempo. tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
puedo, puedes, puede. ¿Puedo...? = may I...? ¿Me puede ayudar?
pronto = soon, temprano = early. ¡Apúrate! = hurry up.
es la una for one o'clock, son las for everything else. y media = half past, y cuarto = quarter past.
¡Amigo! also works as a friendly hail to a stranger.
Señora, ¿me ayuda? doña + first name is the warmer version among neighbours.
¡Señor! to get attention. don + first name is warmer and very LatAm.
¿Cómo está la familia? is a standard courtesy question.
el muchacho is just as common; el niño is a young child.
la muchacha also, though in some countries it means a housemaid.
also means wife in speech: mi mujer.
traer = bring here, llevar = take there. ¿Me trae la cuenta? = could you bring the bill?
está abierto = it's open. Past participle is irregular: abierto.
cierro, cierras. apagar = to switch off. está cerrado = it's closed.
LatAm celular, never Spain's móvil. el teléfono is the landline.
regional: ¿bueno? in Mexico, ¿diga? or ¿sí? elsewhere.
te llamo = I'll call you. marcar = to dial. llamarse = to be called.
platicar (Mexico) and charlar are the words for a chat.
In Mexico and Central America the tortilla is a maize flatbread eaten with everything; in Spain it is an omelette. Further south bread does the job.
arroz con frijoles is the everyday plate across much of LatAm.
frijoles in Mexico and Central America, porotos in the Southern Cone, caraotas in Venezuela. las lentejas = lentils.
los vegetales also heard. la ensalada = salad.
café con leche is the default morning coffee.
sin sal = without salt; salado = salty.
¿Es muy picante? el chile or el ají = chilli. caliente is hot in temperature only.
desayunar = to have breakfast. la merienda = the afternoon snack.
tú: sírvete más. Offering: ¿Le sirvo más?
rico is the everyday word for tasty; delicioso is a notch fancier. ¡Qué rico!
same tener pattern as hambre, frío and calor.
carro in Mexico, Colombia and the Caribbean; el auto in the Southern Cone. Never Spain's coche. manejar = to drive, not conducir.
la habitación is what a hotel calls it. also = a quarter: y cuarto.
the polite word everywhere. Watch the ñ: baño, not bano.
peso in Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Argentina; el sol in Peru, el quetzal in Guatemala. el dólar is widely accepted.
¿Cuánto es? when you are paying up. ¿Cuánto vale? also heard.
tú: espera, or espérame. ¡Pare! = stop! to a driver.
shortens to gran before a singular noun, where it means 'great': un gran día.
chico is commoner in speech. The -ito ending shrinks anything: un cafecito.
quizás and a lo mejor do the same job; capaz que in the Southern Cone.
runs backwards: me gusta el café = coffee pleases me. Plural things take gustan: me gustan los tacos.
the main politeness softener in LatAm speech: un cafecito, ahorita, un momentito, un poquito, despacito.
América Latina is the same thing. Say the country when you can: México, Perú, Colombia, Argentina.
lower case for languages. inglés / inglesa also = English as a nationality.
las maletas = the bags and cases; mis cosas = my stuff.

items.en: present of ser: am, are, is
items.note: estar runs alongside: estoy / estás / está / estamos / están. ser for who or what you are, estar for how or where you are.
bien is the adverb (estoy bien), bueno the adjective (es bueno). Do not swap them.
muchas gracias for warmth. The reply is de nada or no hay de qué.
said to anyone eating, on sitting down or walking past a table. Often clipped to ¡Provecho!
the polite way to order. quiero works but is blunter; me gustaría is the same register as quisiera.
Mucho gusto = pleased to meet you. Con gusto = gladly, and the standard reply to gracias in Colombia.
lo sé = I know that. Ya sé can sound like 'yes, yes, I know' if you are sharp with it.
ni idea = no idea at all. quién sabe = who knows.
the sentence that buys you patience from everyone.
tú: ¿hablas inglés?
tú: ¿de dónde eres? Note ser, not estar.
del Reino Unido = from the UK. Soy inglés / inglesa also works.
estar for location, always. ¿Hay baño? = is there a toilet?
¿Dónde queda...? is very LatAm for places and buildings.
on the phone: Habla Ana. Soy Ana works just as well.
un momentito or un segundito is friendlier.
tú: ¿me puedes ayudar? In an emergency: ¡Ayuda! or ¡Socorro!
also spelt chau. The everyday LatAm goodbye; adiós sounds more final. nos vemos = see you.
tú: cuídate. Warm and very common on parting.
tú: ¿quieres...? Mexico: ¿gusta un cafecito? The hospitality offer you will hear most.
el bebé = baby. mijo / mija is the affectionate address to a child.
LatAm papa, never Spain's patata. las papas fritas = chips.
usted with strangers and elders, and it takes third-person verbs. tú with friends. vos replaces tú in Argentina, Uruguay and much of Central America. The plural is always ustedes, never vosotros.
muchísimas gracias is the same warmth. Answer: con gusto, or no hay de qué.
esto = this, near me; eso = that, near you; aquello = that over there.
de nuevo is the same. ¿Otra vez? on its own = not again!
tacked on the end of a statement. ¿cierto? does the same, especially in Colombia.
blunter and safer: sin chile, or sin picante.
ayudar = to help. ¡Ayuda! shouted is the emergency call.
singular hora even though the answer is plural: son las cinco.
mami and papi are affectionate within a family. Aimed at strangers they can read as flirtation, so keep them for relatives.

items.word: don Carlos / doña María / señor Gómez
items.roman: don Carlos / dona Maria / senor Gomez
items.note: titles go before the name, not after: don and doña with a first name (warm respect, very LatAm), señor and señora with a surname (formal).
feminine but takes el, like el agua. tener hambre = to be hungry.
tengo dinero, tengo tiempo, tengo dos hijos. tener also carries age and hunger: tengo cuarenta años, tengo hambre.
hay covers both is and are: ¿hay wifi? – no hay. Never changes for number.
Pointing in a shop: ¿Me da este? Spanish has no separate word for 'one', so the demonstrative stands alone. No accent on este since 2010.
oiga to a stranger or to usted. Oye is for friends and gets attention without rudeness.
never dropped the way English drops it: creo que sí. Also 'than' in comparisons: más que.
the all-purpose agreement and encouragement token in Argentina, Uruguay and Colombia. Mexico prefers órale or va.
estar + -ando (-ar verbs) or -iendo (-er and -ir verbs). Used far less than English -ing: 'I'm going tomorrow' is voy mañana.
background, habits and descriptions: llovía, éramos jóvenes. The preterite is for finished one-off events.
su is ambiguous, so speech pins it down: el carro de ella, la casa de él.
agrees with the thing owned: nuestra casa, nuestros hijos.
a neat ser/estar test: ¿Cómo es? asks what something is like; ¿Cómo está? asks how it is doing right now.
¿Cuál prefiere? Before a noun Spanish uses qué: ¿Qué color?
masculine despite the -a: buenos días, todo el día.
cuéntame = tell me about it. decir is 'say, tell' for plain information.
pedir is to ask for or order something. Spanish keeps the two apart.
me parece bien = sounds good to me. ¿Qué te parece? = what do you reckon?
duermo, duermes, duerme. tener sueño = to be sleepy.
reflexive: me siento, siéntate, siéntese. Do not confuse with sentirse, to feel.
me levanto a las siete. pararse means 'stand up' in most of LatAm.
a real trap: negative commands switch to the subjunctive even with tú. habla becomes no hables, ven becomes no vengas.
the softest way to ask for something over a counter. Deme is fine but blunter.
essential in LatAm: use it to pass someone, enter a room or leave a table. The reply is propio or adelante.
formal register, for real favours and business. muchas gracias covers everything else.
and the answer is todo bien, gracias. ¿Todo en orden? is the tidier version.
regional variants worth recognising: ¿Qué onda? (Mexico), ¿Qué más? (Colombia), ¿Cómo te va? everywhere.
plural things take gustan: me gustan los tacos. me encanta = I love it.
no accent: si (if) against sí (yes). si quieres, si puede.
the commonest spoken filler after pues. significa = it means.
hoy mismo = this very day, aquí mismo = right here, yo mismo = myself. Also 'same': el mismo día.
rarely needed, since the possessive already does the work: su casa. su propia casa only adds emphasis.

items.en: adjectives agree in gender and number
items.note: and they usually follow the noun: un carro rojo, una casa roja, unos carros rojos.
nos vemos pronto, hasta luego, hasta mañana.
said to someone leaving. tú: que te vaya bien.

items.en: until; up to; as far as
items.note: hasta luego, hasta las cinco. hasta que takes the subjunctive: hasta que llegues.
-er and -ir verbs run comí / comiste / comió / comimos / comieron. Mind the accent: hablo = I speak, habló = he spoke.
speech overwhelmingly uses ir a + infinitive: voy a comer. The -é / -ás / -á forms are commoner in writing and for guesses: será.

items.en: a + el = al, de + el = del
items.note: Nouns never change shape after a preposition; only the article contracts: voy al mercado, la casa del señor. No contraction with the other prepositions.
triggered by wanting, doubt, emotion, and after cuando or para que pointing at the future. Offers use the plain present instead: ¿Te sirvo más?

items.en: the one with; the one from
items.note: el de azul = the one in blue, la de Perú = the one from Peru, el que habla = the one who's speaking.
más de before a number: más de veinte. menos que = less than.
el más barato, la mejor. The -ísimo ending intensifies: buenísimo, carísimo.
ya quedó and listo do the same job. ya está listo = it's ready.
que is never dropped. Softer: me parece que... In the negative it takes the subjunctive: no creo que sea.
tengo que irme = I have to go. ya me voy = right, I'm off.

items.en: could I get some water, please?
items.note: ¿Me trae...? at a table, ¿Me da...? over a counter.
antes de + noun or infinitive: antes de comer. primero = first, in a sequence.
más tarde = later on. luego = then, next.
takes a noun or an infinitive: después de comer, después del trabajo.
antes de las ocho, antes de salir.
para siempre = forever. como siempre = as usual.
de vez en cuando = every now and then.
the double negative is correct Spanish: no voy nunca, no hay nada.
a diario is the tidier version. todas las semanas = every week.
never changes shape: cada día, cada uno. For 'every day' speech prefers todos los días.
no article before it: otro café, never un otro café.
no hay nada, no quiero nada. de nada = you're welcome.
todo bien, todo listo, eso es todo = that's everything.
a las ocho = at eight. Note the a, which ¿Qué hora es? does not take.
media hora = half an hour. ¿Tiene hora? = have you got the time?
cinco minutos. In speech un momentito usually replaces it.
tengo treinta años = I'm thirty. Mind the ñ: año, not ano.
buenos días until midday. en la mañana in LatAm, where Spain says por la mañana.
buenas tardes from midday until dark. There is no separate word for 'evening'.
buenas noches is both 'good evening' and 'goodnight'. anoche = last night.

items.en: the day after tomorrow / the day before yesterday
items.note: anteayer is often antier in Mexico. Neither takes a preposition: te veo pasado mañana.
cien exactly, ciento for 101 to 199: ciento veinte. Then doscientos, trescientos, and the three odd ones: quinientos, setecientos, novecientos.
mil, dos mil. Never un mil. Prices in pesos run into the thousands, so this one earns its keep.
media hora, medio kilo. la mitad is the noun: la mitad del pan.
drops to primer before a masculine noun: el primer día.
mi esposo and mi marido are both everyday.
mi esposa, or simply mi mujer in speech.
los suegros = the in-laws as a pair.
el cuñado = brother-in-law. Spanish has no warm address use like Hindi's भाभी.
los familiares also works. False friend: los padres = parents, not relatives.
los hijos = one's own children: ¿Tiene hijos?
el matrimonio = the marriage; casarse = to get married.
pienso, piensas, piensa. pensar en = think about; pensar que = think that.
estoy aprendiendo español.
ir de compras = to go shopping.
leo, lees, lee. estudiar is 'to study'; la lectura is reading as an activity.
¿Me lo escribe? = could you write it down for me? – very useful for addresses.
mándame un mensaje. enviar is the tidier twin; mandar also means 'to order someone about'.
salgo, sales, sale. salir de = leave from. la salida = the exit.
llegar a = arrive at. la llegada = arrival.
¿Le ayudo? = shall I give you a hand?
intentar is the same. probar = to try or taste something.
empieza a las ocho. comenzar is the formal twin.
se acabó el agua. ya terminó = it's over, of an event.
the blame-free construction Spanish prefers, as if it forgot itself. Olvidé is also fine.
se corta = you're breaking up. usted: no lo escucho bien.
usted: le llamo más tarde. The plain present does duty as a future here.
LatAm te extraño; te echo de menos is Spain.
sin azúcar = no sugar. Also used as an endearment in the Caribbean.
los dulces = sweets. el postre = pudding.
me duele la panza is what people actually say for a tummy ache.
llena if you are female. Softer refusal at a table: ya quedé bien, gracias.

items.word: Soy alérgico a … / Soy alérgica a …

items.en: to him, to her, to you (formal), to them

'Entre A y B' for between two things.

'Donde mi tía' in Colombia and Chile; 'en casa de mi tía' everywhere.

Two words. 'Sino' as one word means 'but rather'.

items.en: softening a request with the conditional or imperfect

items.en: to carry on; to keep doing; to still be doing
items.note: Siga derecho = carry straight on. sigo esperando = I'm still waiting. sigo, sigues, sigue.
